attachments.origin_landmark: calcaneus (medial and lateral heads, flanking the long plantar ligament)
attachments.insertion_landmark: flexor digitorum longus tendon (inserting onto the tendon itself, not bone)

actions: corrects flexor digitorum longus's oblique line of pull to a purely anteroposterior direction

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Unusual among skeletal muscles for inserting onto a tendon rather than bone; exists specifically to correct FDL's diagonal pull (since the human foot's long axis doesn't align with the leg's midline the way FDL's tendon does).
functional_compartments.source: Ward SR, Eng CM, Smallwood LH, Lieber RL (2009) Clin Orthop Relat Res 467:1074-1082 -- lower-extremity muscle architecture (fascicle length, PCSA, sarcomere length) cadaver dataset

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Ward SR, Eng CM, Smallwood LH, Lieber RL (2009) Clin Orthop Relat Res 467:1074-1082 -- lower-extremity muscle architecture (fascicle length, PCSA, sarcomere length) cadaver dataset

trigger_points.location_description: Deep in the second plantar layer of the foot, beneath flexor digitorum brevis, spanning from the calcaneus to its insertion on the flexor digitorum longus tendons.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Pain distributed over the plantar heel and the medial-to-central sole of the foot, contributing to plantar heel pain; the deep location means the pain is often felt as a poorly localized ache rather than a sharply defined zone.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Prolonged weight-bearing, walking on hard/uneven surfaces, and a compromised or overloaded plantar arch.
trigger_points.notes: In a case-control study of chronic plantar heel pain, active trigger points in quadratus plantae were the single most prevalent finding (62.5% of patients), more common than in matched healthy controls, and their referred pain reproduced the patients' clinical symptoms; can mimic plantar fasciitis or tibial nerve (tarsal tunnel) compression.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual, Vol. 2 (Lower Extremities), 1999 -- as cited in secondary summaries (e.g. Morningside Acupuncture NYC 'Quadratus Plantae Trigger Points') describing the deep plantar-heel/sole referral pattern; prevalence and clinical association in plantar heel pain per Ortega-Santiago R, Rios-Leon M, Martin-Casas P, Fernandez-de-Las-Penas C, Plaza-Manzano G (2020) 'Active Muscle Trigger Points Are Associated with Pain and Related Disability in Patients with Plantar Heel Pain: A Case-Control Study.' Pain Med 21(5):1032-1038, doi:10.1093/pm/pnz086 -- retrieved via PubMed
